changes.before: Implement titlePatch(body). Match the worked contract and the changed-input checks without modifying the supplied input values.
changes.after: Copy only the fields a caller is allowed to change.

before: A validated request can still contain fields the caller must not control. Build the write object from an explicit list of permitted fields.
This exercise is a small pure JavaScript model. Its inputs are supplied directly; it does not receive live HTTP requests, operate a database, or deploy a service.
The object literal creates a new object with only title. Spreading the entire body would also copy ownerId or admin. This step assumes title was already validated.

Read the function call titlePatch({"title":"Moon","ownerId":"attacker"}) from the inside out: the arguments supply the inputs, titlePatch runs the body once, and return sends its result back to the caller. console.log displays that result; it does not change it.
Why not use {...body} for this update? An allowlist determines writable fields. Ownership must come from a trusted session and stored record.
after: An update should contain only the fields the caller may change. An allowlist names those permitted fields. This update allows title, and nothing else.
This step assumes title has already been checked. It chooses which field to copy; it does not check the caller's identity or permission to edit the record.
{title: body.title} creates a new object with one field. It reads the supplied title without changing the original body.

Copying the whole body with {...body} could also copy ownerId or admin. Those extra fields must not become writable just because the caller included them. A real server checks ownership using trusted identity and stored data.
Complete titlePatch(body) by returning a new object containing only title. Preserve its already-checked value exactly, and leave all other supplied fields out.
